claim: T cell activation requires engagement of a cognate antigen by the T cell receptor (TCR) and the co-stimulatory signal of CD28.
source: T cell activation requires engagement of a cognate antigen by the T cell receptor (TCR) and the co-stimulatory signal of CD28.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in immunology supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Both TCR and CD28 aggregate into clusters at the plasma membrane of activated T cells.
source: Both TCR and CD28 aggregate into clusters at the plasma membrane of activated T cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: Upon CD28 triggering, the BAR-domain protein sorting nexin 9 (SNX9) is recruited to CD28 clusters at the immunological synapse.
source: Here, we report that upon CD28 triggering, the BAR-domain protein sorting nexin 9 (SNX9) is recruited to CD28 clusters at the immunological synapse.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SNX9 generates membrane tubulation out of CD28 clusters.
source: Using three-dimensional correlative light and electron microscopy, we show that SNX9 generates membrane tubulation out of CD28 clusters.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlative light and electron microscopy data presented in Figure 4.

claim: CD28 clusters are dynamic structures.
source: Our data further reveal that CD28 clusters are in fact dynamic structures and that SNX9 regulates their stability as well as CD28 phosphorylation and the resulting production of the cytokine IL-2.
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation and FRAP experiments shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: SNX9 regulates CD28 cluster stability.
source: Our data further reveal that CD28 clusters are in fact dynamic structures and that SNX9 regulates their stability as well as CD28 phosphorylation and the resulting production of the cytokine IL-2.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experiments comparing WT and SNX9 KO cells shown in Figure 5.

claim: SNX9 regulates CD28 phosphorylation.
source: Our data further reveal that CD28 clusters are in fact dynamic structures and that SNX9 regulates their stability as well as CD28 phosphorylation and the resulting production of the cytokine IL-2.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced CD28 phosphorylation in SNX9 KO cells (Figure 7A-B).

claim: SNX9 regulates IL-2 production.
source: Our data further reveal that CD28 clusters are in fact dynamic structures and that SNX9 regulates their stability as well as CD28 phosphorylation and the resulting production of the cytokine IL-2.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data showing reduced IL-2 secretion in SNX9 KO cells (Figure 7D).

claim: SNX9-mediated tubulation generates a membrane environment that promotes CD28 triggering and downstream signalling events.
source: In summary, our work suggests a model in which SNX9-mediated tubulation generates a membrane environment that promotes CD28 triggering and downstream signalling events.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the collective experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Priming of naive T cells requires an additional costimulatory signal delivered by CD28.
source: Priming of naive T cells requires an additional costimulatory signal delivered by CD28 (Boomer and Green, 2010; Esensten et al., 2016; Rudd et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Upon binding of the ligands CD80 and CD86 at the surface of professional antigen-presenting cells, CD28 recruits several effector proteins including filamin-A, Grb2, PI-3K, and PKCθ.
source: Upon binding of the ligands CD80 and CD86 (otherwise known as B7-1 and B7-2) at the surface of professional antigen-presenting cells, CD28 recruits several effector proteins including filamin-A, Grb2, PI-3K, and PKCθ.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of T cell biology.

claim: CD28 triggering promotes T cell activation through cytoskeletal rearrangements, the nuclear translocation of the transcription factor NFAT and the secretion of interleukin-2 (IL-2).
source: Ultimately, CD28 triggering promotes T cell activation through cytoskeletal rearrangements, the nuclear translocation of the transcription factor NFAT and the secretion of internleukin-2 (IL-2) (Sanchez-Lockhart et al., 2004; Fraser et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In absence of CD28 signalling, naive T cells fail to activate and fall into a permanent state of unresponsiveness known as anergy.
source: In absence of CD28 signalling, naive T cells fail to activate and fall into a permanent state of unresponsiveness known as anergy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on T cell anergy.

claim: Anergy is characterised by the inability to produce IL-2 and proliferate.
source: Anergy is characterised by the inability to produce IL-2 and proliferate (Harding et al., 1992; Jenkins et al., 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to foundational studies on T cell anergy.

claim: CD28 signalling promotes cytokines transcription independently of TCR.
source: CD28 signalling also promotes cytokines transcription independently of TCR (Raab et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: T cell activation by antigen-presenting cells leads to the formation of a specialised cell-cell interface, the immunological synapse.
source: T cell activation by antigen-presenting cells leads to the formation of a specialised cell-cell interface, the immunological synapse (Rossy et al., 2012; Davis and Dustin, 2004).
evidence: This is well-established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Stimulation of TCR and CD28 is required to localise CD28 within the immunological synapse.
source: Stimulation of TCR and CD28 is required to localise CD28 within the immunological synapse (Sanchez-Lockhart et al., 2008), whose formation is impaired in absence of CD28 co-simulation (Wülfing et al., 2002; Huang et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Formation of the immunological synapse is impaired in absence of CD28 co-stimulation.
source: Stimulation of TCR and CD28 is required to localise CD28 within the immunological synapse (Sanchez-Lockhart et al., 2008), whose formation is impaired in absence of CD28 co-simulation (Wülfing et al., 2002; Huang et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Localisation and activation of CD28 at the synapse are required to trigger downstream signalling events required for productive T cell activation.
source: Furthermore, localisation and activation of CD28 at the synapse are required to trigger downstream signalling events required for productive T cell activation (Sanchez-Lockhart et al., 2008; Tseng et al., 2005; Yokosuka et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Within the immunological synapse, surface receptors, signalling and adaptor proteins assemble in protein clusters, which are essential for the initiation and amplification of T cell signalling.
source: Within the immunological synapse, surface receptors, signalling and adaptor proteins assemble in protein clusters, which are essential for the initiation and amplification of T cell signalling (Campi et al., 2005; Varma et al., 2006; Rossy et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: T cell activation or engagement of CD80/86 leads to CD28 clustering.
source: Accordingly, T cell activation or engagement of CD80/86 leads to CD28 clustering, which is driven only by interactions within the extracellular domain of CD28 (Tseng et al., 2005; Tseng et al., 2008; Yokosuka et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CD28 clustering is driven only by interactions within the extracellular domain of CD28.
source: Accordingly, T cell activation or engagement of CD80/86 leads to CD28 clustering, which is driven only by interactions within the extracellular domain of CD28 (Tseng et al., 2005; Tseng et al., 2008; Yokosuka et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TCR and CD28 clusters are spatially segregated within the immunological synapse.
source: Importantly, TCR and CD28 clusters are spatially segregated within the immunological synapse (Tseng et al., 2005; Tseng et al., 2008), which suggests that they might have distinct properties and regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TCR and CD28 clusters might have distinct properties and regulatory mechanisms.
source: Importantly, TCR and CD28 clusters are spatially segregated within the immunological synapse (Tseng et al., 2005; Tseng et al., 2008), which suggests that they might have distinct properties and regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial segregation of TCR and CD28 clusters.

claim: SNX9 is a BAR-domain protein that stands at the interface between the plasma membrane and intracellular membranes.
source: Sorting nexin 9 (SNX9) is a BAR-domain protein that stands at the interface between the plasma membrane and intracellular membranes (Bendris and Schmid, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: SNX9 binds to specific areas of membranes through a curvature-sensitive BAR domain and a phosphoinositides-interacting pleckstrin homology (PX) domain.
source: SNX9 binds to specific areas of membranes through two types of domains: a curvature-sensitive BAR domain (Shin et al., 2008) and a phosphoinositides-interacting pleckstrin homology (PX) domain (Pylypenko et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The SH3 domain of SNX9 recruits N-WASP, an activator of the Arp2/3 actin nucleating complex.
source: The SH3 domain of SNX9 recruits N-WASP, an activator of the Arp2/3 actin nucleating complex (Yarar et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2008) and the membrane scission protein dynamin (Lundmark and Carlsson, 2003; Shin et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The SH3 domain of SNX9 recruits the membrane scission protein dynamin.
source: The SH3 domain of SNX9 recruits N-WASP, an activator of the Arp2/3 actin nucleating complex (Yarar et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2008) and the membrane scission protein dynamin (Lundmark and Carlsson, 2003; Shin et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The low complexity domain of SNX9 mediates interactions with components of the actin polymerisation and clathrin-mediated endocytosis machineries such as clathrin, AP-2 and Arp2/3.
source: The so-called low complexity domain of SNX9 mediates further interactions with components of the actin polymerisation and clathrin-mediated endocytosis machineries such as clathrin, AP-2 and Arp2/3 (Lundmark and Carlsson, 2003; Shin et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Unidentified domains of SNX9 link it to the small GTPases RhoA and Cdc42.
source: Unidentified domains of SNX9 also link it to the small GTPases RhoA and Cdc42 (Bendris et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SNX9 activity is related to localised actin polymerisation and formation of tubular invaginations of the plasma membrane.
source: Hence, SNX9 activity is related to localised actin polymerisation and formation of tubular invaginations of the plasma membrane (van Weering et al., 2012; Yarar et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2008), often in the context of clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Lo et al., 2017; Schöneberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SNX9 plays a role in many cellular processes that involve membrane remodelling, such as the formation of the apical domain of polarised cells, macropinosome formation, phagosome maturation, or invadopodia formation.
source: SNX9 plays a role in many cellular processes that involve membrane remodelling, such as the formation of the apical domain of polarised cells (Román-Fernández et al., 2018), macropinosome formation (Wang et al., 2010), phagosome maturation (Almendinger et al., 2011), or invadopodia formation (Bendris et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SNX9 expression is decreased in T cells upon inflammation.
source: SNX9 expression is decreased in T cells upon inflammation (Ish-Shalom et al., 2016) and has been implicated in CD28 endocytosis (Badour et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SNX9 has been implicated in CD28 endocytosis.
source: SNX9 expression is decreased in T cells upon inflammation (Ish-Shalom et al., 2016) and has been implicated in CD28 endocytosis (Badour et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SNX9 was present at the immunological synapse from 2 min onwards after T cell activation.
source: A blinded analysis of the localisation of SNX9 revealed that it was present at the immunological synapse from 2 min onwards, where it was detected in 75% ± 7.6% of the conjugates after 15 min of activation (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: SNX9 was detected in 75% ± 7.6% of the conjugates after 15 min of activation.
source: A blinded analysis of the localisation of SNX9 revealed that it was present at the immunological synapse from 2 min onwards, where it was detected in 75% ± 7.6% of the conjugates after 15 min of activation (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SNX9 was enriched close to the cover glass at the immunological synapse, identified by the signal of TCRζ-EGFP.
source: 3D reconstructions showed that SNX9 was enriched close to the cover glass at the immunological synapse, identified by the signal of TCRζ-EGFP (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by 3D reconstruction data from live cell imaging shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SNX9 recruitment to the immunological synapse was confirmed in primary T cells interacting with dendritic cells.
source: We further confirmed the recruitment of SNX9 to the immunological synapse in primary T cells interacting with dendritic cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from primary CD4+ T cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over 70% of the CD4+ T cells showed SNX9 recruitment to the synapse when activated by peptide-pulsed BMDCs.
source: We observed a clear recruitment to the synapse, here identified by CD28, in over 70% of the CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of primary T cell data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: SNX9 was completely cytosolic in resting cells, where not a single SNX9-positive structure was detected over four independent experiments.
source: Strikingly, SNX9 was completely cytosolic in resting cells, where not a single SNX9-positive structure was detected over four independent experiments.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of SNX9-positive structures shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Stimulation of CD28 alone and co-stimulation of CD28 and TCR were about twice as potent as TCR triggering alone in stimulating the formation of SNX9-positive structures.
source: Stimulation of CD28 alone and co-stimulation of CD28 and TCR were about twice as potent as TCR triggering alone in stimulating the formation of SNX9-positive structures.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of SNX9-positive structures under different activation conditions shown in Figure 1E.

claim: CD28 stimulation during T cell activation promotes the formation of SNX9-positive structures at the immunological synapse.
source: Thus, it is possible that organisation of the plasma membrane by SNX9 within CD28 clusters contributes to establish a distinct lipid environment within CD28 clusters and, by doing so, promotes cluster stability and signalling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased SNX9-positive structures upon CD28 stimulation.

claim: The membranous structures positive for SNX9 were detected just above the immunological synapse within a narrow peak around 0.9 µm from the 0 μm position.
source: Strikingly, the membranous structures positive for SNX9 were detected just above the immunological synapse within a narrow peak around 0.9 µm from the 0 μm position, immediately after the peak defined by the CD28 clusters and yet closer to the synapse than TCR or Rab5 endosomes.
evidence: This is supported by axial distribution analysis of SNX9, CD28, TCRζ, and Rab5 structures shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: SNX9 intracellular structures were below TCR and Rab5-positive endosomes.
source: This analysis confirmed that SNX9 intracellular structures were below TCR and Rab5-positive endosomes.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of axial positions shown in Figure 1H.

claim: SNX9 is not associated with endosomes in resting cells but rather decorates structures strictly proximal to the immunological synapse upon T cell activation.
source: In summary, these experiments show that SNX9 is not associated with endosomes in resting cells but rather decorates structures strictly proximal to the immunological synapse upon T cell activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial distribution analysis of SNX9 relative to endosomal markers.

claim: Both CD28WT and CD28YF were organised in clusters within the plasma membrane.
source: In accordance with previous publications (Tseng et al., 2005; Tseng et al., 2008; Yokosuka et al., 2008), both CD28WT and CD28YF were organised in clusters within the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and citations to previous studies.

claim: SNX9 was also clustered at the immunological synapse.
source: Crucially, SNX9 was also clustered with line profiles of fluorescence intensity across the cell (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data and fluorescence intensity profiles shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The majority of clusters defined by SNX9 overlapped with CD28 clusters.
source: We used an intensity-based threshold analysis identifying clusters in each channel to confirm that the majority of clusters defined by SNX9 overlapped with CD28 clusters (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was a clear tendency of a lower overlap of SNX9 clusters with the non-phosphorylatable form of CD28 when compared to WTCD28.
source: While not significant, we observed a clear tendency of a lower overlap of SNX9 clusters with the non-phosphorylatable form of CD28 when compared to WTCD28, suggesting that CD28 phosphorylation may contribute to the recruitment of SNX9.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of colocalization shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CD28 phosphorylation may contribute to the recruitment of SNX9.
source: While not significant, we observed a clear tendency of a lower overlap of SNX9 clusters with the non-phosphorylatable form of CD28 when compared to WTCD28, suggesting that CD28 phosphorylation may contribute to the recruitment of SNX9.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed trend in colocalization data.

claim: CD28 clusters remain co-localised with clusters of SNX9-EGFP after photoactivation.
source: Photoactivation of CD28-PAmCherry at the plasma membrane by TIRF 405 nm illumination also revealed that CD28 clusters remain co-localised with clusters of SNX9-EGFP after photoactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CD28-EGFP arrives at the immunological synapse first, recruiting SNX9-mCherry over time to the same microclusters.
source: CD28 clusters were first observed in 'ridges' of plasma membrane mediating the first contacts of the cell with the stimulatory surface, as previously described for clusters of Lat in activating T cells (Sherman et al., 2011). SNX9 was first found in the cytosol within these ridges and clusters of SNX9 were detected approximately 50 s later (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: SNX9 is recruited to pre-existing CD28 clusters, as opposed to CD28 being recruited to SNX9 clusters.
source: Thus, these time-sequence experiments establish that SNX9 is recruited to pre-existing CD28 clusters, as opposed to CD28 being recruited to SNX9 clusters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal dynamics observed in time-lapse imaging.

claim: SNX9 is not required to establish CD28 clusters upon T cell activation.
source: These results further indicate that SNX9 is not required to establish CD28 clusters upon T cell activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CD28 clusters form before SNX9 recruitment.

claim: SNX9 recruitment into CD28 clusters requires the functional domains of SNX9 conferring interaction with proteins containing proline-rich motifs and membranes.
source: Thus, SNX9 recruitment to CD28 clusters is not mediated by phosphorylated tyrosine residues on CD28 but requires the functional domains of SNX9 conferring interaction with proteins containing proline-rich motifs and membranes.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with SNX9 deletion mutants shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: SNX9 recruitment to CD28 clusters is not mediated by phosphorylated tyrosine residues on CD28.
source: Thus, SNX9 recruitment to CD28 clusters is not mediated by phosphorylated tyrosine residues on CD28 but requires the functional domains of SNX9 conferring interaction with proteins containing proline-rich motifs and membranes.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing SNX9 recruitment to both CD28WT and CD28YF clusters.

claim: Interactions with clathrin or AP-2 are not sufficient to locate SNX9 in CD28 clusters.
source: Importantly, because the low complexity domain which binds to clathrin and AP-2 (Lundmark and Carlsson, 2009) is still present in the ΔSH3-SNX9 mutant, our results suggest that interactions with clathrin or AP-2 are not sufficient to locate SNX9 in CD28 clusters.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ΔSH3-SNX9 mutant is not recruited to CD28 clusters despite retaining the low complexity domain.

claim: SNX9 localisation in CD28 clusters is independent of the clathrin endocytic machinery.
source: The fact that the ΔSH3-SNX9 mutant was not recruited to CD28 clusters despite having been shown to be normally recruited to clathrin coated pits (Schöneberg et al., 2017) further indicates that SNX9 localisation in CD28 clusters is independent of the clathrin endocytic machinery.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential behavior of ΔSH3-SNX9 mutant in CD28 clusters versus clathrin-coated pits.

claim: SNX9 diffused rapidly throughout the immune synapse, while predominantly co-localising with the clustered signal of CD28.
source: This quantification revealed that SNX9 diffused rapidly throughout the immune synapse, while predominantly co-localising with the clustered signal of CD28.
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The signal of SNX9-PAmCherry was significantly higher in clusters than in the cytosol within 4 s after the beginning of 405 nm illumination.
source: The signal of SNX9-PAmCherry was significantly higher in clusters than in the cytosol within 4 s after the beginning of 405 nm illumination.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of photoactivation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SNX9 at the plasma membrane in CD28 clusters is not incorporated into endocytic vesicles.
source: This observation suggests that SNX9 at the plasma membrane in CD28 clusters is not incorporated into endocytic vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of SNX9-PAmCherry-positive endosomal structures after photoactivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: The fluorescence intensity of photoactivated SNX9-PAmCherry in the mask defined by CD28-EGFP did not decrease significantly over a time period of 10 min.
source: The fluorescence intensity of photoactivated SNX9-PAmCherry in the mask defined by CD28-EGFP did not decrese significantly over a time period of 10 min, indicating that SNX9 is stably associated with CD28 clusters over time.
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation and time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: SNX9 is stably associated with CD28 clusters over time.
source: The fluorescence intensity of photoactivated SNX9-PAmCherry in the mask defined by CD28-EGFP did not decrese significantly over a time period of 10 min, indicating that SNX9 is stably associated with CD28 clusters over time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the photoactivation persistence data.

claim: SNX9 molecules are rapidly exchanged between CD28 clusters but nevertheless remain strictly incorporated within the population of CD28 clusters.
source: Collectively, these data reveal that SNX9 molecules are rapidly exchanged between CD28 clusters but nevertheless remain strictly incorporated within the population of CD28 clusters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined photoactivation experiments showing rapid diffusion but stable association.

claim: Abundant tubules were present within the tomographic section volume of activated T cells.
source: Tilt series were acquired, and the 3D reconstruction showed abundant tubules present within the section volume (E i – E iv; Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CD28 clusters were highly abundant and present at the immune synapse and matched well with the undulations of the plasma membrane.
source: 3D correlation showed the CD28 clusters were highly abundant and present at the immune synapse and matched well with the undulations of the plasma membrane (z = 0 nm, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by correlative light and electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: SNX9 decorated and defined long tubular structures emerging from the immunological synapse within the tomographic volume.
source: The fluorescence signal of the SNX9 decorated and defined long tubular structures emerging from the immunological synapse within the tomographic volume (z = 100 nm, Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by correlative light and electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The SNX9 tubules arose from the CD28 clusters at the plasma membrane.
source: Strikingly, the SNX9 tubules arose from the CD28 clusters at the plasma membrane (Figure 4H–J).
evidence: This is supported by correlative light and electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4H-J.

claim: SNX9-positive tubules had an average diameter between 80 and 100 nm.
source: These structures had an average diameter between 80 and 100 nm, which is consistent with previous observation made with reconstituted tubules in vitro (van Weering et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on measurements from electron tomography data and is consistent with previous in vitro studies.

claim: SNX9-positive tubules showed a clear tendency to be larger than SNX9-negative tubules, being significantly longer.
source: SNX9-positive tubules showed a clear tendency to be larger than SNX9-negative tubules, being significantly longer (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of tubule dimensions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: SNX9 is enriched in tubules emanating from CD28 clusters on the plasma membrane and promote their elongation in activated T cells.
source: In summary, these high-resolution analyses and quantification suggest that SNX9 is enriched in tubules emanating from CD28 clusters on the plasma membrane and promote their elongation in activated T cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electron tomography and quantitative analysis of tubule dimensions.

claim: CD28 was not detected within SNX9 tubular structures.
source: As we did not detect CD28 within these tubular SNX9 structures, we speculate that their function is to regulate the presence of lipids or specific effectors within CD28 clusters, and thereby mediate CD28 signalling as detailed below in the discussion.
evidence: This is based on the correlative microscopy data showing spatial separation of CD28 and SNX9 tubules.

claim: The function of SNX9 tubules is to regulate the presence of lipids or specific effectors within CD28 clusters, and thereby mediate CD28 signalling.
source: As we did not detect CD28 within these tubular SNX9 structures, we speculate that their function is to regulate the presence of lipids or specific effectors within CD28 clusters, and thereby mediate CD28 signalling as detailed below in the discussion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Mutations of tyrosine residues in the YF mutant had no impact on the number of CD28 clusters.
source: Mutations of tyrosine residues in the YF mutant had no impact on the number of CD28 clusters as previously published (Yokosuka et al., 2008), nor did the knock-out of SNX9 (Figure 5A), indicating that SNX9 is not required for CD28 to assemble into clusters.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of CD28 clusters shown in Figure 5A and B, and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: The knock-out of SNX9 had no impact on the number of CD28 clusters.
source: Mutations of tyrosine residues in the YF mutant had no impact on the number of CD28 clusters as previously published (Yokosuka et al., 2008), nor did the knock-out of SNX9 (Figure 5A), indicating that SNX9 is not required for CD28 to assemble into clusters.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of CD28 clusters shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: SNX9 is not required for CD28 to assemble into clusters.
source: Mutations of tyrosine residues in the YF mutant had no impact on the number of CD28 clusters as previously published (Yokosuka et al., 2008), nor did the knock-out of SNX9 (Figure 5A), indicating that SNX9 is not required for CD28 to assemble into clusters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantitative analysis of CD28 clusters in SNX9 KO cells.

claim: When photoactivated with 405 nm light at the periphery of the cells, CD28-PAmCherry diffused rapidly through the entire activation area while remaining strictly within clusters.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that when photoactivated with 405 nm light at the periphery of the cells, CD28-PAmCherry diffused rapidly through the entire activation area while remaining strictly within clusters (Figure 5C; Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TCRζ-PAmCherry underwent moderate diffusion within the plasma membrane before being quickly internalised within endocytic vesicles.
source: By contrast, TCRζ-PAmCherry underwent moderate diffusion within the plasma membrane before being quickly internalised within endocytic vesicles as previously reported (Figure 5C; Figure 5—video 1; Compeer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments shown in Figure 5C and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: Even though CD28 clusters appear very stable, CD28 is constantly exchanged within the population of clusters.
source: This result reveals that even though CD28 clusters appear very stable (Figures 2 and 3), CD28 is constantly exchanged within the population of clusters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the photoactivation experiments showing rapid diffusion of CD28 between clusters.

claim: The recovery rate of fluorescence in CD28 clusters of cells overexpressing SNX9 was significantly lower than the recovery rate of control cells from 94 s on.
source: Divergence analysis revealed that the recovery rate of fluorescence in CD28 clusters of cells overexpressing SNX9 was significantly lower than the recovery rate of control cells from 94 s on.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data and divergence analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CD28WT-EGFP clusters had recovered 57.4% ± 10.9% of their initial fluorescence in WT cells without SNX9 transfection and only 34.6% ± 4.8% of fluorescence in cells overexpressing SNX9.
source: Plotting the mean of the fluorescence intensity profiles at 380 s after initial photobleaching further showed that CD28WT-EGFP clusters had recovered 57.4% ± 10.9% of their initial fluorescence in WT cells without SNX9 transfection and only 34.6% ± 4.8% of fluorescence in cells overexpressing SNX9 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of FRAP data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: SNX9 promotes the stability of CD28 clusters.
source: This suggests that SNX9 promotes the stability of CD28 clusters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP data showing reduced fluorescence recovery in cells overexpressing SNX9.

claim: Fluorescence intensity within CD28 clusters recovered significantly faster in both SNX9 KO Jurkat T cell lines.
source: In line with this, fluorescence intensity within CD28 clusters recovered significantly faster in both SNX9 KO Jurkat T cell lines, diverging significantly from the WT control recovery curve at 124 and 384 s after bleaching in two SNX9 KO clones.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data and divergence analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The percentage of CD28-EGFP fluorescence recovery at 380 s was higher in SNX9 KO cells than for WT cells, reaching 70.4% ± 4.7% and 69% ± 13%.
source: This was further illustrated by the fact that the percentage of CD28-EGFP fluorescence recovery at 380 s was higher in SNX9 KO cells than for WT cells (57.4%), reaching 70.4% ± 4.7% and 69% ± 13%.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of FRAP data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The absence of SNX9 in the knock-out cell lines did not alter CD28 expression.
source: Of note, these differences were not the result of differential expression of CD28, as the absence of SNX9 in the knock-out cell lines did not alter CD28 expression (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data measuring CD28 surface expression shown in Figure 6.

claim: There was no significant difference in the FRAP of clusters of CD28WT and CD28YF.
source: There was no significant difference in the FRAP of clusters of CD28WT and CD28YF, indicating that unlike SNX9, phosphorylation of the intracellular domains of CD28 does not contribute to CD28 cluster stability.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data comparing CD28WT and CD28YF shown in Figure 5.

claim: Phosphorylation of the intracellular domains of CD28 does not contribute to CD28 cluster stability.
source: There was no significant difference in the FRAP of clusters of CD28WT and CD28YF, indicating that unlike SNX9, phosphorylation of the intracellular domains of CD28 does not contribute to CD28 cluster stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP data comparing CD28WT and CD28YF.

claim: The fluorescence signal recovered in bleached areas of Lck10-EGFP within seconds and reached 89.2% ± 4.4% of the maximal signal at 380 s.
source: In contrast to the fluorescence recovery for CD28 (57.4%), the fluorescence signal recovered in bleached areas within seconds and reached 89.2% ± 4.4% of the maximal signal at 380 s (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data for Lck10-EGFP shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: There were no significant differences in the FRAP of Lck10 upon overexpression or knock-out of SNX9.
source: More importantly, there were no significant differences in the FRAP of Lck10 upon overexpression or knock-out of SNX9, confirming the specificity of the effect of SNX9 on CD28 cluster stability.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data for Lck10-EGFP in different SNX9 conditions shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The effect of SNX9 on CD28 cluster stability is specific.
source: More importantly, there were no significant differences in the FRAP of Lck10 upon overexpression or knock-out of SNX9, confirming the specificity of the effect of SNX9 on CD28 cluster stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of FRAP data for CD28 and Lck10.

claim: Cell surface expression and internalisation of CD28 did not differ significantly between Jurkat WT and SNX9 KO in resting or activated cells.
source: Cell surface expression and internalisation of CD28 did not differ significantly between Jurkat WT and SNX9 KO in resting or activated cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data measuring CD28 surface expression and internalization shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: SNX9 does not regulate CD28 internalisation from the cell surface in Jurkat T cells.
source: To compensate for the difference in CD28 surface expression between the various KO cell lines, we calculated the normalised ratio between surface expression and uptake of CD28-FITC fluorescence signal, which confirmed that SNX9 does not regulate CD28 internalisation from the cell surface in Jurkat T cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of CD28 internalization shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Extensive endocytosis of CD28 does not occur in activated T cells.
source: Our data globally suggest that extensive endocytosis of CD28 does not occur in activated T cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including lack of intracellular CD28 vesicles and low rates of CD28 internalization.

claim: After 10 min of activation only 42.8% ± 5.7% of the initial levels of cell surface TCR could still be detected at the cell surface, in contrast to 88.8% ± 7.3% for CD28.
source: After 10 min of activation only 42.8% ± 5.7% of the initial levels of cell surface TCR could still be detected at the cell surface, in contract to 88.8% ± 7.3% for CD28 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data measuring surface levels of TCR and CD28 over time shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: SNX9 does not significantly contribute to the moderate internalisation of CD28.
source: In summary, our observations indicate that SNX9 does not significantly contribute to the moderate internalisation of CD28.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CD28 internalization assays in WT and SNX9 KO cells.

claim: CD28 phosphorylation is maximal around 5 min after activation and persists for at least 30 min.
source: CD28 phosphorylation is the first detectable event in CD28 triggering. It is maximal around 5 min after activation and persists for at least 30 min (Sadra et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Both SNX9 KO cell lines showed a significant decrease of CD28 phosphorylation (40% ± 19.2%) compared to WT cells.
source: Both SNX9 KO cell lines showed a significant decrease of CD28 phosphorylation (40% ± 19.2%) compared to WT cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data measuring phosphorylated CD28 shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of phosphorylated TCR did not differ between WT and SNX9 KO cells.
source: By contrast, the fluorescence intensity of phosphorylated TCR did not differ between WT and SNX9 KO cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data measuring phosphorylated TCRζ shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: SNX9 specifically contributes to the phosphorylation of CD28 upon T cell activation.
source: Thus, SNX9 specifically contributes to the phosphorylation of CD28 upon T cell activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of SNX9 KO on CD28 versus TCR phosphorylation.

claim: There was significantly less NFAT in the nucleus of SNX9 KO cells compared to WT cells upon activation.
source: Quantification of the levels of NFAT co-localizing with the nucleus using a dedicated analysis routine (Schindelin et al., 2012) revealed that there was significantly less NFAT in the nucleus of SNX9 KO cells compared to WT cells upon activation (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: There was a significant decrease of IL-2 secretion from the SNX9 KO cells (an average of 2.20 ng/ml for WT, 1.34 ng/ml for SNX9 KO#3 and 1.17 ng/ml for SNX9 KO#4) compared to WT cells.
source: We observed a significant decrease of IL-2 secretion from the SNX9 KO cells (an average of 2.20 ng/ml for WT, 1.34 ng/ml for SNX9 KO#3 and 1.17 ng/ml for SNX9 KO#4) compared to WT cells.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data measuring IL-2 secretion shown in Figure 7D.

claim: SNX9 is specifically required for CD28 triggering and downstream cellular events upon T cell activation.
source: Taken together, these data on the functional consequences of SNX9 knock-out show that SNX9 is specifically required for CD28 triggering and downstream cellular events upon T cell activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective functional data showing effects on CD28 phosphorylation, NFAT translocation, and IL-2 secretion.

claim: Adaptor proteins regulate stability of T cell clusters and thereby determine the intensity of T cell activation.
source: It has been shown that adaptor proteins regulate stability of T cell clusters and thereby determine the intensity of T cell activation (Lasserre et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Regulation of cell surface expression modulates receptor signalling.
source: Regulation of cell surface expression modulates receptor signalling and SNX9 plays a role in CD28 internalisation (Badour et al., 2007).
evidence: This is general knowledge in cell biology supported by a citation.

claim: Very modest rates of CD28 endocytosis occur in activated T cells.
source: However, our data suggests very modest rates of CD28 endocytosis occur in activated T cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CD28 internalization assays and imaging data.

claim: SNX9 knock-out had no impact on CD28 surface expression.
source: Furthermore, SNX9 knock-out had no impact on CD28 surface expression.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6.

claim: SNX9 can recruit and activate the actin nucleating complex Arp2/3 through its SH3 domain.
source: Another possible mechanism of regulation of CD28 signalling by SNX9 in clusters could be via the control of actin polymerisation, as SNX9 can recruit and activate the actin nucleating complex Arp2/3 through its SH3 domain (Yarar et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In T cells, actin is required for TCR cluster formation at the immunological synapse.
source: In T cells, actin is required for TCR cluster formation at the immunological synapse (Campi et al., 2005) and, more generally, can regulate cluster stability (Lavi et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CD28 signalling is connected to actin polymerisation.
source: CD28 signalling is also connected to actin polymerisation (Tavano et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The assembly of CD28 clusters does not involve actin polymerisation.
source: Yet, the assembly of CD28 clusters does not involve actin polymerisation (Yokosuka et al., 2008) and they have never been described as actin-rich structures.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Membrane heterogeneity and local enrichment of lipid species have been shown to regulate many aspects of T cell signalling and activation.
source: Indeed, membrane heterogeneity and local enrichment of lipid species have been shown to regulate many aspects of T cell signalling and activation.
evidence: This is general knowledge in the field of T cell biology.

claim: Diacylglycerol at the synapse promotes T cell polarity.
source: Diacylglycerol at the synapse promotes T cell polarity (Chauveau et al., 2014) and phosphoinositides control actin organisation (Le Floc'h et al., 2013; Gawden-Bone et al., 2018) and TCRζ accumulation (DeFord-Watts et al., 2011) at the immunological synapse.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phosphoinositides control actin organisation at the immunological synapse.
source: Diacylglycerol at the synapse promotes T cell polarity (Chauveau et al., 2014) and phosphoinositides control actin organisation (Le Floc'h et al., 2013; Gawden-Bone et al., 2018) and TCRζ accumulation (DeFord-Watts et al., 2011) at the immunological synapse.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phosphoinositides control TCRζ accumulation at the immunological synapse.
source: Diacylglycerol at the synapse promotes T cell polarity (Chauveau et al., 2014) and phosphoinositides control actin organisation (Le Floc'h et al., 2013; Gawden-Bone et al., 2018) and TCRζ accumulation (DeFord-Watts et al., 2011) at the immunological synapse.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Phosphatidylserine and phosphoinositides play a central role in TCR triggering by favouring the release of intracellular domains of the TCR-CD3 complex from the plasma membrane.
source: More importantly, phosphatidylserine (Gagnon et al., 2012) and phosphoinositides (Chouaki Benmansour et al., 2018) play a central role in TCR triggering by favouring the release of intracellular domains of the TCR-CD3 complex from the plasma membrane.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A model has been put forward in which intracellular domains are inaccessible to effectors while bound to the inner leaflet to explain CD28 triggering.
source: This model, in which intracellular domains are inaccessible to effectors while bound to the inner leaflet, has also been put forward to explain CD28 triggering (Dobbins et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is possible that organisation of the plasma membrane by SNX9 within CD28 clusters contributes to establish a distinct lipid environment within CD28 clusters and promotes cluster stability and signalling.
source: Thus, it is possible that organisation of the plasma membrane by SNX9 within CD28 clusters contributes to establish a distinct lipid environment within CD28 clusters and, by doing so, promotes cluster stability and signalling.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Several BAR-domain proteins can cluster phosphoinositides and generate lipid domains.
source: Several BAR-domain proteins can cluster phosphoinositides and generate lipid domains (Picas et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2013; Saarikangas et al., 2009), although this has not yet been described for SNX9.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies, but notes this has not been shown for SNX9.

claim: Membrane curvature is thought to promote formation of specific lipid subdomains by driving the enrichment of lipids that preferentially associate with the curvature of the local membrane.
source: Membrane curvature, like the SNX9-positive tubules that we observed at the synapse, is also thought to promote formation of specific lipid subdomains by driving the enrichment of lipids that preferentially associate with the curvature of the local membrane (Callan-Jones et al., 2011; Parton et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Membrane curvature induced by SNX9 tubulation would favour membrane detachment of the CD28 cytoplasmic domain and provide improved access of CD28 intracellular domain to effectors.
source: This would favour membrane detachment of the CD28 cytoplasmic domain and, in doing so, would provide improved access of CD28 intracellular domain to effectors.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed based on the structural findings and known effects of membrane curvature.

claim: Membrane curvature can favour clustering of proteins.
source: However, membrane curvature can favour clustering of proteins (Reynwar et al., 2007; Strahl et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Membrane curvature induced by SNX9 tubulation in CD28 cluster could promote recruitment and clustering of CD28 effectors to facilitate CD28 phosphorylation and signalling.
source: Therefore, membrane curvature induced by SNX9 tubulation in CD28 cluster could promote recruitment and clustering of CD28 effectors to facilitate CD28 phosphorylation and signalling.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed based on known effects of membrane curvature on protein clustering.

claim: Curvature is postulated to influence diffusion of membrane proteins in theoretical models.
source: Aside from clustering, curvature is postulated to influence diffusion of membrane proteins in theoretical models (Yoshigaki, 2007; Balakrishnan, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Slower diffusion at CD28 clusters increases the dwell time of CD28 effectors and potentiates CD28 signalling.
source: We speculate that slower diffusion at CD28 clusters increases the dwell time of CD28 effectors and by doing so potentiates CD28 signalling as it has been recently shown for SOS and N-WASP (Martin and Mittag, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed based on recent findings about dwell time effects on signaling.

claim: Membrane curvature can directly regulate enzymatic activity, including of proteins that are reported effectors of CD28.
source: Finally, membrane curvature can directly regulate enzymatic activity, including of proteins that are reported effectors of CD28.
evidence: This is general knowledge about the effects of membrane curvature on enzyme activity.

claim: The activity of phosphoinositide 3-kinase, which is recruited to the YMNM motif on the cytoplasmic tail of CD28 upon triggering, is increased by membrane curvature.
source: The activity of phosphoinositide 3-kinase, which is recruited to the YMNM motif on the cytoplasmic tail of CD28 upon triggering, is increased by membrane curvature (Bettache et al., 2003; Hübner et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Curvature has been shown to modulate the activity of PKC, another key effector of CD28 signalling.
source: Similarly, curvature has been shown to modulate the activity of PKC, another key effector of CD28 signalling (Goldberg and Zidovetzki, 1998; Jiménez-Monreal et al., 1999; Epand and Lester, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CD28 clusters at the immunological synapse recruit SNX9 upon CD28 triggering.
source: In summary, in this study we show that CD28 clusters at the immunological synapse recruit SNX9 upon CD28 triggering.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: SNX9 generates membrane tubulation at CD28 clusters.
source: We present evidence that SNX9 generates membrane tubulation at CD28 clusters and regulates their stability and we establish a clear link between SNX9, and CD28 phosphorylation and downstream signalling in T cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: There is a clear link between SNX9, and CD28 phosphorylation and downstream signalling in T cells.
source: We present evidence that SNX9 generates membrane tubulation at CD28 clusters and regulates their stability and we establish a clear link between SNX9, and CD28 phosphorylation and downstream signalling in T cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: The results suggest a revised model of lipid organisation at the immunological synapse, in which membrane-binding protein would organise the composition and curvature of the membrane at T cell microclusters.
source: Our results suggest a revised model of lipid organisation at the immunological synapse, in which membrane-binding protein would organise the composition and curvature of the membrane at T cell microclusters.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the collective findings of the study.

claim: Lipid organisation inside clusters could be central to how signalling is regulated within these structures.
source: They further suggest that lipid organisation inside clusters could be central to how signalling is regulated within these structures.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.
